segments.translation: I call myself Sallie Margaret Christie Luethje.
In Cherokee now.
My name is ᏥᎩᎥ. ᏥᎩᎥ is my real given name. I have two names and in Creek, they call me Tobi.
Really? Are you part Creek, too?
No. When he was married to my mom, and I guess it was my step-dad, he was Creek, but my dad was a Christie.
Where were you born?
Tahlequah.
Tahlequah.
At Hastings.
About when were you born?
December 31st, 1947.
Where.. And where did you grow up?
Stilwell, towards Peavine.
Is that the only place you lived, or somewhere else? Did you all move around?
Nowhere else, that’s the only place I grew up. As of Mom, she grew up towards ᎧᏬᏂ and Spade mountain, they call it, she grew there.
Did you work?

Yeah, I looked after older people for 10 years. I watched after older people. And then when they opened up the school Flaming Rainbow, I finished there. Then I started working at the Jack Brown Center. I watched the kids who used stuff to get drunk and high, like I looked after them for 25 years. I worked.
That was a long time, wasn’t it?
A long time. That’s where I fell and broke my shoulder. That’s when they put a new artificial on. Then I had to quit.
Is it good now?
Not really, it’s not good. I can’t do things I used to do nowadays. But I keep going. Sometimes, when it’s cloudy, it still bothers me sometimes.
How many siblings do you have?

I was by myself. I have two half-brothers. But they were way older when I was growing up. I was born last. They were from ᎦᏣᏃᏍᏗ and ᎨᎱᎦ. My dad had different women. The first one he was married to, when she passed away, he got with my mom and then I was born. One of the boys was run over by a train, Jack Christie, around Marble City. My other brother, Bob Christie, he was half white. His mom was a white. My dad worked on the railroads. He didn’t have time to look after a baby boy. He put him in Sequoyah, because Sequoyah had orphans. He grew up there. And he passed away, too. It’s been about three years since he left. He never forgot how to talk Cherokee. He was talking Cherokee, and he was half white. He talked good Cherokee.
Who… who were your parents?
My parents?
Yeah.

ᎦᏣᏃᏍᏗ was my dad’s name, Richard Christie. I didn’t know where he was really from. Marble City is what my mom used to say. That’s all I know. I was five years old when he passed. He used to work on the railroad, and what they call TB was going around. And he caught it, and it killed him, my dad. As for my mom, her mom was Eva Swimmer and her dad was Alex Hair. Sally Hair, they called my dad. I meant my mom, excuse me, I was wrong. My mom is Sally Hair.
What about your grandma and your grandpa?

My grandma was Eva Swimmer on my mom’s side. And Alex Hair was my grandpa on my mom’s side. On my dad’s side, it’s written on the ancestor papers I have. I think Tacky was my grandma’s name, Tacky Christie. And my grandpa’s name, Chicken Toter Christie is what they called him. They had different names, they were from North Carolina.
Really?
They’re buried in Dwight Mission.
Really?
Yeah.
Did they go to school there?

I don’t know why they were buried there. My dad was old when I was born. They’re really old, because it wasn’t just a little while ago when they died, it was really a long time ago. They died over 35 years ago. 35 – they went through the Trail of Tears.
What about your second last name? Is that something to talk about?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Where did it start from?
Where did it start from, your second last name?
Christie?
Yeah.

I would talk about that for a long time. And these days, I don’t know, because like I said, Dad died when I was five years old. And he wasn’t home very much, because he worked on the railroad. He was always leaving, then he would always come back. On weekends, he would leave again when the trains were leaving. I did know a lot about where he came from, that’s all I was saying about the ancestry papers I have about Tacky Christie and Chicken Toter is what he was called. If I had brought them, I would have known their full names. William Christie is what I think they called him. As I’ve been reading, they were from North Carolina. My dad had a roll number. I guess he was just a little boy when he was brought here. I think they came on the Trail of Tears.
And they came here.

They came here. He came as far as Marble City. Mom grew up around Peavine. ᎫᏬ they called Mulberry Holler. She grew up there. Mom was from Eva Swimmer Blackwood on my grandmother’s side. On my dad’s side was a Tacky, that’s all I knew his name was.
What about when you were growing up, what relatives were there?
Family? Just family, or who? All of us as a group, as a community?
Yeah, those who lived near your house.

His name was John Blackwood. He was related to all of my mom and them. They called her Tlanen, but her name was Nutsi. Nutsi came from the Scrapers. When they got married, she became a Blackwood, when she married John. John and Nancy Blackwood. Ned Bean, Ned and Josie Bean. There in Mulberry, they were all friends. If someone died, they would go visit them at their house and stay with them two or three weeks. Watching that sick person, they did not think, “Just let it go, let it be.” They watched the elders. They weren’t old then, they were younger. The women cooked and the men just watched out for them and got water. We didn’t have water inside and no inside bathroom. It isn’t like it is right now.
That John Blackwood you were saying, was he a preacher?

I’m talking about his dad. John Blackwood Junior’s dad. Junior is the preacher but that old man I was talking about, he was a Christian and that’s how much he helped people. He would always walk, and they would just go walk to help people. We were all related there at Peavine. Marie Jane Crittenden was her name. There were a lot of us, and they helped each other out. I was just a child, about five. They did the same for my dad. They watched him every day until he passed. When he took his last breath, they were all sitting and holding his hand. That's the way it was back then. We loved each other. It’s not like that today.
Even around midnight they would go.

Yeah, even at midnight. Somebody would call them to come, but there were no phone sounds. We didn’t have phones, never made a sound. We never had things like that. He would just come walking, even if it was midnight, and if they did, it was important. He wasn’t just drunk, standing there. There were a lot of drunks walking around. They kept to themselves somewhere. They were whooping around.
What about the food you all ate? Now what did y’all make to eat?

Well, a long time ago, the way white people looked at natives, they would say, “They’re letting those cows out,” when we were looking for new growth when it was almost summer, like mushrooms. We were looking for green things to eat. We would eat that in the spring. We were dependent on that, and the men would hunt. About three would go hunting. They would take what they call gunnie sacks, and they would kill squirrels for us. And rabbits they would kill for us and give them to us. They would kill them and give all of them to the people. That's how I said we helped each other and made it through. And also, they would make a garden. Every summer they would have a garden, and they canned. It was hard work. I was just little, and I was thinking I was helping. I was learning to do that. Like canning tomatoes, and we had lots of beans canned. What they called peas. We were canning all of those to help us in the winter. It was really pretty. We lived in a log cabin, a two-room log cabin. Really… that’s what we lived in. It leaked when it rained, and where the eaves were, it was full of onions. We had them hanging there. They dug deep in the ground to store turnips and filled it up with potatoes. We always had something to eat. And then, if they went hunting, they would kill a lot of things to eat. We never ate deer, just rabbits, squirrels, and quail. Things like that were helpful to us. In the summertime, we’d go to Peavine Creek. Peavine Creek, we would go up three hills. We'd go to the river, and we would take skillets to cook with. Like beans, we would cook there by the water. If they caught crawdads, we would cook them right there. And they would always gig and catch fish. We would just eat them by the creek. We would clean up good, and walk back up the hill. We would take everything after we ate. And when we got back, we would already have been sweating, when we got to the house. That's how it was back then.
It’s not like that nowadays, is it not?

Huh-uh. A long time, that was helpful to us. A lot of those big farmers, like when they raised strawberries or beans, we would leave at five in the morning. We would get in the car, Chewy Watt was his name, he took us to where we worked. Sometimes, we made $0.50 an hour. Sometimes we’d work all day and would just make $2.00. I learned from following the grownups, and I learned from following the elders, too. When they went to work, I would work, too. I was about seven or eight years old when I started working. When the time came for me to drive a car, when we got one, I learned to do that, too. I know a lot of things that we done. I know a lot of things that we did with the elders. Mom used to drink. Sometimes when she would drink, she.. Someone would have to drive the car. But I watched all of them.
And you drove?
Yeah, I learned to.
How old were you back then?
I was around eight when I started.
You were driving?

Yeah, and when I learned how to speak English, I translated for them. I am amazed by this, I feel sorry for them, these Hispanic children. You have seen them in stores, haven’t you? When they’re trying to help their parents speak. That's what I went through. They didn’t speak or understand English. They done them back when they took land away from them, ain’t it?
Yeah.
But that’s different now.
It’s different now, ain’t it? Did you ever play ball when you were growing up?

Yeah, let me see. I just played around at school. I didn’t play until I got to the fifth grade. Those older girls taught me. I just went around quietly, just ourselves. It was extremely bad for us. The two white families lived there, and we were together with them. I would help them, I was feeling bad for them and helped them. We would just run around there. Them girls chose me and they said, “Let’s play ball.” I told them I didn’t know how. I was just in the fifth grade, and they were in the eighth grade. They said, “Try, let’s play.” They stood me out there. I tried and I was holding on to the bat, and the ball went by really fast. It scared me. “Haw," I thought, “what am I going to do? This is embarrassing,” I was thinking to myself. But they didn’t care. They said, “Keep on trying,” and then Lueanne Bean, Ned Bean’s daughter – we are related – and she said this to me and put her arm around me, “You hit that ball,” she told me. “I’m sitting right here, I’m not going anywhere, and I'll be watching you.” My head got this [gestures] big, and I really hit it. And it went way out of sight, and that’s when I started.
Did you go all the way around?

Yeah, I went all the way around. That’s what I used to hit, home runs. That went by pretty good. All the way through grade school. We did good, us girls. And I taught the other girls, Kenny Hogner’s girl, Reba was her name. She started in fourth grade, too. That is where we started, fourth grade. We played together. Then, when we got to high school, they didn’t let us play that much. The rich people’s kids played, and they wouldn’t choose us. But when they practiced (ᎠᎾᎵᏏᎾᎯᏍᏗ) they would use us. But when they played, they didn’t allow us to play.
They didn’t know you could hit hard. How many kids do you have?
Seven.
Seven. Are they all alive?
Yeah, they’re all alive. The oldest one I have is deaf.
What about your grandkids?
Haw, 33, I think. We're waiting for the tenth great-grandchild. It’ll be here in August. A baby girl.
What about... What about when they hear you speak Cherokee, who do they think you sound like?
If I speak Cherokee from a long time ago?
You speaking Cherokee.

When I was growing up in Peavine a long time ago, only the elders spoke Cherokee, and I mostly followed them around. I warned them, but they already spoke English in school. They couldn’t speak Cherokee, but could sing in Cherokee. But they wouldn’t let them. They wouldn’t let them sing in Cherokee, and they forgot all of it. They didn’t speak Cherokee, but when we went to high school, Charlie Soap and I went to school here, and he never spoke Cherokee. And Leroy, too, we played ball together. We never talked Cherokee, we always talked English. I tried talking Cherokee to him, but he told me he didn’t understand.
He didn’t understand?

They would say, “I don’t understand. I don’t know what you are saying,” they would say. And I would just let it go and just keep talking Cherokee sometimes. But some of the ones that were from Bell, some of the children were learning when I got to the ninth grade. Then we became friends, and we would all talk Cherokee. I was depending on them to speak Cherokee. I felt good, because I was thinking about quitting. I was thinking about that when we met trying to get our driver’s licenses. And the boys didn’t know what to write on their paper, and they were looking at mine. I gave them a strange look, and I asked them, “Y’all don’t know what to write?” to see what they were going to say. And one got close to me and showed me his paper, and he copied from mine. And we all passed.
So you were helping them.
They never did forget. I was telling Bub Locust, “Boy we really did cheat,” and that was how we got our driver’s licenses, I told him.
Is that one from Bell, Bub Locust, that you’re talking about?
I don’t know where he is now. He went to a lot of different places.
This Cherokee that they’re talking, in 20 years, what do you think from what you see, will come to the Cherokee language?

This is what I think. It won’t ever be like we speak, like me and you are speaking. It never happens like that. It’s because no one taught us. No one ever taught me to speak Cherokee, and also, nobody taught me to do good for people. I just learned from watching my mom. From the elders speaking, I picked it up there, you would say. That was all I talked, and that was all I spoke, and that was all I knew, was Cherokee. These that are growing up, I don’t know what they’re going to do. Those that are raising five but the mother and father have to both learn Cherokee, that is what I think. And that child will learn better, because it can’t be just half of it, with just the child speaking. They really have to be fluent in teaching these children. They can’t throw around English. There were a lot of whites that came through that wanted to learn, but they were learning the way we were talking Cherokee. There was a guy I knew in Stilwell named Rufus Thomas, he had a taxicab, and he could speak good Cherokee.
He was white, wasn’t he?
Yeah, he was Caucasian. Ruby’s sister was married to Goodlow Sams. Ruby spoke Cherokee, too.
I remember that. They would speak in all Cherokee.

Yeah, they spoke in all Cherokee. They would be laughing like that, and they would never treat anybody bad. They were really friendly; they picked that up, too. My husband, Arnold, he’s a German, but he thinks like a Cherokee, cause we’re always together. We’ve been together 50 years. When June 6th comes, we will have been together 51 years.
Y’all have been together 51 years. Does he understand Cherokee?

He understands Cherokee, he doesn’t really speak, but he speaks a little bit. I think he can speak more, but I think he’s a little bit afraid of me, I think. But the way he thinks, he thinks in Cherokee, and what I’m saying is true. And the children that I have, they think Cherokee, and when you see them, you think they’re going to speak in Cherokee. But I never did teach them Cherokee. I wanted something better to happen to them. I didn’t want them to go through what I went through because we all love each other. We want better things to happen to them. I think now I should’ve taught them Cherokee, but I don’t think they could ever learn it good now. They might learn a little bit, but not everything. But I think we’re going in the right direction, teaching the little kids and babies. If the parents help them, I believe the little kids will learn Cherokee, is what I think about the kids. I’ve talked to some of them that are in there. They’re trying to talk. I feel like it’s going to happen.
What about the parents who don’t speak Cherokee?
This is what I tell them. Nona Buress, do you know her?

My daughter Eva, her husband’s mom, passed away. That's when I met these little boys and I was trying them out and talking to them in Cherokee. They answered me, so I said, “Y’all speak Cherokee?” And they said yes. “I go to school,” one said. He was a fifth grader. And the fourth grader didn’t answer back. He didn’t hardly say nothing. But that fifth grader, we had quite a conversation. Both of us, he said, that one standing right there can speak Cherokee, he said. He did pretty good, talking. I talked to him good and his mom doesn’t speak. She just speaks in English. I don’t know, his dad may speak, I don’t know. But his mom doesn’t. She just speaks in all English.
I know Cody.
Really?
That’s your grandkid, right?
Cody Buress.
Yeah.
Yeah, my grandson.
He works at the clinic. He's a friendly boy.

Yeah. So is the other one they call Donald. Donald Luethje. He worked as a locksmith, or I guess you could say electrician. My son and Eva, my daughter. Eva Buress they called her, my daughter, they both been working 30 years at Hastings. I guess it’s the same for you, ain’t it?
Yeah, pretty close.
You two know each other, huh?
Us two are gonna get old. What about this… in about 25 years, do you think the trees and woods are gonna be there?

We’re in bad times, really bad. Nowadays, we realize it. We can’t even go into the woods anywhere anymore with a runny nose. Some people have running noses that won’t stop. And even their eyes, they swell up when they go outside. That is pollution. It’s the trees that heal us. Water, too. All of water. They’re building chicken houses and bringing in a lot of cows. They’re killing the earth. I don’t know what’s going to happen that far ahead. We're in dangerous times.
That’s already happening, huh? And all on the side of the roads.
We can’t even go swimming anymore, it’s all fenced up.
You can’t even catch as many crawdads as you want.

I don’t know if they’re any good anymore. The water isn’t any good. We used to get watercress anywhere. They said right here you could get a lot of watercress. In the evenings, it would be good food to eat. And these days, I don’t know if it’s good now.
What about medicine in the woods, did they ever teach you anything about stuff like that?

Not that kind, but I knew a little bit about the medicine. I didn’t know that much about the roots. Just to boil them, I guess, just things like that. I don’t know everything, because no one ever taught me. That Nancy Hogner they called her, she was an old lady. She raised me as if she was my grandma. I never went to the doctor. They just went and got her when I was sick. She would stay two or three days doctoring me. She would doctor me with fire. She would warm my chest, and I remember I would start feeling better. Sometimes I thought I had pneumonia. Because the belief that we had is what some of them used. When they would touch our hearts, we would liven up. It’s the same today, because you can’t get well from someone just touching you with their hands. Someone has to touch you or hug you to get over it. It’s still like that today, but it’s not happening. It’s sad that we lost the old people. I think I’m probably going to go through that myself. Sometimes it really scares me. It’s sad. A long time ago, like I was saying earlier, my dad, they were all holding on to him when he died. He went to a better place is what I think. If you yourself are scared, it’s a scary thing to die. It'll scare you.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Is that all?
Now, me and you are finished up. Is there something?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Do you want to say something about someone or something?

That, and we just talked about everything I’ve always wanted to talk about, and I may have to talk English. “Generational.” Do you two know what I said? Bringing in alcohol, it was sad what happened, when they gave it to them. When they gave it to the elders. They just wanted to take the land away. So nowadays, we don’t have anything. We can’t even go swimming, it’s always fenced in. We're doing good… He gave us love for one another. And they took everything, then. A long time ago, that Sweptson. They were all farmers across the road. He bought a little bit of land, and my grandma had a lot of land, Eva Swimmer. That’s where I grew up. I remember when my mother was drinking, when they wanted a little money, they’d sell a little land. They didn’t think nothing of it. They didn’t know, they didn’t understand what they were selling. I remember that there Fats Sweptson, he was a cop. When he got there, he was fencing some of it up. He’d say, “I don’t want the cows to get in your garden, I’m just going to fence this much up,” he said when he started. He kept fencing, and he got all the land. When I grew up, I could understand a little English. I found out, if they put those fences up, in seven years, it would be theirs. They couldn’t do that because it was restricted land. Grandma had a roll number. They couldn’t take it from her – it was restricted land. The BIA workers were cheating. That’s why they lost a lot of land. That’s why I’m thankful for the chief we have right now. I think he’s gonna do something. He's gonna help us if they help him. If there’s a chief, you’re supposed to help him. You’re not supposed to go against him. So maybe good things will happen to us. You can stop progress, what the white people call progress. That's why I didn’t teach the kids Cherokee. I didn’t get taken advantage of, like they were taking advantage of the elders. Odie Worliy’s tavern, I don’t think none of them are alive. Nobody ever walked by, and I really mean what I said. Some of them would laugh at each other. When I was growing up, they would laugh at me, but I couldn’t do anything, I was just a kid. If I was in there, I couldn’t do anything. That’s why I didn’t care if they were laughing at me. I didn’t care if the elders were laughing at me, I still cared for them. The compassion I have, I learned it from them. I felt sorry for the elders. That’sw here I learned it. And I’m old, I’m old. And I still feel sorry for them, the young men who are just growing up, the next generation. They’re having troubles. They're having a hard time making it through. They call it meth, that is killing them, the teenage boys, and we don’t do anything to help them. And this chief in there, he listened to what I said. I told him we need to help them, my boy as well. It’s happening to him. And they took him today, he asked to go himself. He said, “I’m not ready, I’m not ready to get out.” He told me, “I’m gonna go back to work over there. I ain’t got no life here,” he said. I was glad that he was going to do that. Today, they took him back. CARES, they call it, in Jay, OK. They really use God over there. He prays. He has love, that boy, he really has love for people. But when he’s drinking or using, you can’t recognize him. That’s what’s happening to them. A lot of women’s kids, elders are raising the kids. It’s sad what’s happening to the kids. The mothers don’t even care what’s happening to the kids. They'll just say, “Mom is watching the kid.” They don’t know when their mom is going to die. It’s sad the way we are living. All of us Indians need to help each other. Pretty soon, nobody is going to help us. Anybody. The whites aren’t going to help us. There’s a lot of that going on in the world, they call it racism, that’s happening. They’re talking about it everywhere. We need to listen to what’s happening around the world. If Jesus is talking to you, you need to listen. This past Sunday, a redbird was crying out on the porch. It was really crying out. A long time ago, they used to say someone is going to visit you. When I get up, I tell God, “Haw, I’m gonna get up.” When I get up, you too, get up. And some of them, the white people, we talk to them. When we say we’re talking to them, the animals, it’s not that way from my understanding. It’s not like that, I wasn’t talking to the bird, and it wasn’t talking back to me. Because I have God in me, it was touching me and I was touching it, is what I thought. I was just touching this much. That’s how we were talking. Not while I’m on earth, while I’m alive. I don’t know what is going to happen when he takes me up above. I think he’s gonna take me sometimes. He’s gonna take all of us. We got to be ready, and we got to understand, and we need to know him. We could talk to him every day. We just watch. He’s gonna help us.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: That it?
I guess so.
